beats.narration_text: Three props for Walker Rudy, assembled from basic shapes. Nobody sculpted them, and no model generated a mesh. Claude moved cubes, cones and cylinders in a running Blender, shuai-z made one edit by hand, and Godot measured the result.

beats.act: the game and the three props
beats.narration_text: Walker Rudy is a 2D side-scroller. Rudy crosses Level 1, the Harvest Fields, and these are the three props on his way: spikes, which cost him a heart; the waystone, where he gets back up; and the teleport circle that ends the level. Here they are from the game's own files, all at one scale. Rudy is a hundred and sixty pixels tall, so shuai-z set him at one point two metres, and every size in the brief comes from these pixels.

shot.observation: The game's own 2D files drawn at one scale on a common ground line: Rudy (160 px), the spikes, the lit waystone and the teleport circle, each labelled with its role in Level 1.

beats.narration_text: Before anything was built, the brief was committed. Each prop in metres, its origin at the centre of its underside so it stands on the floor, its shapes and a triangle budget. And six failures, predicted with a way to catch each: lying on its side, because Blender is Z-up and Godot is Y-up, the wrong size by a factor, a floating origin, too many triangles, a colour lost in export, and more detail than asked.

beats.act: one prompt → the code Claude ran
beats.narration_text: Here is one prompt and what it did. The waystone's rune had become a capital R, and shuai-z wrote: it does not look good now; no R, try a ring. Claude answered with code, run inside that Blender. An eight-sided cylinder, twenty-two centimetres across, two centimetres deep, turned to lie flat against the stone at the height shuai-z had chosen by hand. Every one of these calls is kept, in order, in the tools folder.

beats.narration_text: And this is what it built: Blender's own viewport, captured by Claude through the MCP's look tool, not a screenshot shuai-z took. A blue ring with a stone-coloured disc in its middle. A torus is not one of the course's basic shapes, so the ring is two cylinders.

beats.act: the hand edit — before and after
beats.narration_text: Before any of that came the hand edit. Left, the rune as Claude built it. Right, the saved file after shuai-z moved it in Blender's window: G, then Z, then a drag. G starts a move and Z locks it to the vertical axis. Three point four centimetres up. These are comparison stills, not a recording; no recording of the edit was made. What it taught: Blender's keys are a sequence, not a chord.

shot.observation: Front views from the MCP look tool: before (19:58 EDT, as built, rune centre Z 0.42) and after (the saved hand-edited file, rune centre Z 0.4537); the guide lines mark the rune's top in each.

beats.narration_text: The whole cycle. A plain rectangle, moved by hand. An R, which went over budget and was rejected on sight. An eight-sided ring, then twelve sides and a thinner band, kept. That pushed the waystone from forty-two triangles to a hundred and eighteen, past the brief's sixty, so revision two raised the budget to a hundred and thirty and said why. Revision one stays as it was.

beats.narration_text: The other two, built the same way. The teleport circle is three stacked discs and three rune marks. While planning it, Claude found that all three undersides would share the floor plane and flicker from below, which the brief had missed, so revision three lifted two of them. The spikes are a wooden block and five eight-sided cones. Two hundred eighty triangles of three hundred, and eighty-two of a hundred.

beats.act: the scene — one line per prop
beats.narration_text: Each prop was exported as its own glb file, with Blender's plus Y up option, and loaded into a new Godot project. A script builds the scene. Look at the table: a name, a file and an X position, and no height at all. Every prop goes in at Y equals zero. That only works because each origin is the centre of the prop's underside. And a one point two metre post stands in for Rudy, so the sizes can be judged.

props.title: Placing Three Props on One Floor
props.code:
## name, scene, X position (m). Each origin is the centre of the prop's
## underside, so Y = 0 puts it on the floor.
const PROPS := [
	["Spikes", "res://assets/props/spikes.glb", -2.0],
	["Waystone", "res://assets/props/waystone.glb", -0.8],
	["TeleportCircle", "res://assets/props/teleport_circle.glb", 1.2],
]

const RUDY_HEIGHT := 1.2 ## m, CHANGE-BRIEF.md: Rudy = 160 px = 1.2 m

beats.narration_text: The check. It loads each glb on its own, with no window, and measures its bounding box. Width, depth and height must match the brief within five millimetres. Then the lines that catch two predicted failures. Which axis carries the height? Upright means only Y does, which catches the lying-on-its-side failure. And the centre of the underside must sit at the origin, or the prop would float or sink.

beats.narration_text: These are headless numbers, run again for this film. Brief, Blender and Godot agree: point seven by point four by point eight four for the waystone, to four decimal places. Every height is on Y, every origin is at zero, every count is inside its budget. Forty-four checks, zero failed. Read the last line, not the exit code: when the first version of this script would not even parse, Godot still exited with zero.

beats.act: the check — sitting on the floor
beats.narration_text: The second part loads the scene itself. It finds the floor's top from the floor mesh, not from the prop, and then asks, for each prop, how far its lowest point is above it. In Module 3, an agent's floor check measured the object against its own collider and proved nothing. So: can this one fail?

beats.narration_text: Yes. On an isolated copy, the waystone was raised thirty centimetres in the scene file, and nothing else changed. The check reports it, fails, and exits with one. A test of the test, not the game; the project's scene was never touched.

shot.observation: Recorded output: the scene as built passes (lowest point 0.0000 m); an isolated copy with the waystone's transform Y set to 0.3 reports 'FAIL Waystone sits on the floor (lowest point 0.3000 m above the floor's top)', 'FAIL: 1 failed check(s)', exit code 1.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked by machine: sizes, axis, origin, scale, triangles and colours, forty-four checks, and the check can fail. Checked by a person: shuai-z walked the camera round, behind and below. The sizes suit the post, and the spikes look most like the 2D art; the teleport circle least, with no rune pattern, no light and no glow. Uncertain: no one else has looked, it ran only on a Mac, and the scene is not yet joined to the game. What Claude got wrong: the brief missed the undersides, the first check never ran, and the first screenshot was taken from the wrong place.

artifactLines: Machine: 44 headless checks pass on godot/ at f6f8acf (re-run for this film on an isolated copy); with the waystone raised 0.3 m, the floor check fails, exit code 1.
Human: shuai-z looked in the Godot editor, from behind and below: sizes suit the 1.2 m post; the gold is brighter in Godot than in Blender; spikes closest to the 2D art, the teleport circle furthest.
Uncertain: no second viewer; macOS only; Blender sizes read by code, not from the sidebar; the scene is separate from the 2D game.
Claude got wrong: the brief missed the circle's undersides (revision 3); the first check had parse errors yet exited 0; the first screenshot read the camera before the scene was in the tree.

beats.narration_text: Who made what. shuai-z chose the props, approved the brief and every build step, made the hand edit, rejected the R and chose the ring, and did the human check. Claude drafted the brief, wrote and ran every Blender call through the MCP, the export, the Godot scene, the check and this film. The source shown is f six f eight a c f. The next step is the teleport circle: its rune pattern, its column of light and its glow.
